**C.3  Avian Review**

## **Review of Avian Studies in the Tehachapi Wind Resource Area Kern County, California**

_Prepared for:_

CH2M HILL, Inc.

_Prepared by:_

Wallace Erickson, Andrea Chatfield  and Kimberly Bay

**W** estern **E** co **S** ystems **T** echnology, Inc.

2003 Central Avenue Cheyenne, Wyoming

June 10, 2009

## **TABLE OF CONTENTS**

## **LIST OF FIGURES**

## **INTRODUCTION**

Alta Windpower Development, LLC (Alta Windpower) is proposing to develop the Alta-Oak Creek Mojave Project (Project) in the Tehachapi Wind Resource Area (TWRA), located in Kern County, California. CH2M HILL, a contractor to Alta Windpower, requested that Western EcoSystems Technology, Inc. (WEST) provide a summary and peer review of the relevant avian and bat resource data that is available or is currently being collected that will be useful for predicting and evaluating the potential impacts of the proposed project on birds and bats. This memorandum contains our review of the relevant site-specific and regional information for these purposes.

## **AVIAN STUDIES**

## **Site Specific Studies**

## _M.H. Wolfe and Associates – 2007/2008_

M.H. Wolfe and Associates conducted baseline wildlife studies in the three Subareas, the CPC East, the CPC Proper, and the Ward Subareas, which comprise the larger Project (Figure 1; M.H. Wolfe and Associates 2009a, 2009b, 2009c). Avian survey work was conducted from February 2007 through December 2008 and included bird use counts, sensitive species surveys, and nest searches.

Bird use counts were conducted quarterly (spring, summer, fall, winter), from April 2007 through September 2008. Bird counts consisted of a series of observation points, placed at a minimum distance of 825 feet (ft; 251.5 meters [m]) apart, along trails, roads or utility corridors traversing each of the three subareas. Each observation point was surveyed for five minutes (min), during which all birds observed were recorded, along with the number of individuals, distance from the point, and the flight height. Bird use counts were conducted in the morning from approximately 15 min before sunrise until 10:30 a.m. Additional late morning/afternoon raptor counts were added in April of 2008, which used the same survey locations and methods as for bird use counts but were conducted from in late morning/early afternoon, or 10:30 a.m to 3:00 p.m.

Approximately 73 hours of bird observations were made during seven visits to 125 points within the CPC East Subarea from April 2007 through September 2008. During these surveys, 1,620 individual birds were observed representing 50 species. Twenty-four individual raptors (1.5% of overall bird observations) representing four species were recorded. Within the CPC Proper Subarea from July 2007 through September 2008, approximately 18 hours of observations were made during six visits to 36 points. A total of 1,255 individual birds representing 26 species were recorded, of which 15 individuals comprising two species were raptors. Another 18 hours of observations were made at the Ward Subarea during seven visits to the 30 points established at this location from April 2007 through September 2008. At the Ward Subarea, 1,310 individual bird species representing 31 species, of which 27 individuals comprising three species were raptors. Based on the avian use data collected, M.H. Wolfe and Associates predicted impacts to individual bird species, including sensitive species, would not be significant for most species.

However, combined with other existing wind-energy developments, cumulative significant impacts to raptors such as golden eagle ( _Aquila chrysaetos_ ) and burrowing owl ( _Athene cunicularia_ ), may be possible with the addition of the proposed Project.

Sensitive species surveys and nest searches were conducted throughout the study area by walking meandering transects approximately 60 feet (18.3 m) apart throughout areas known to be directly impacted by the proposed facility. Additional raptor nest searches were conducted in cliff/rock habitats using binoculars. No state or federal threatened species were recorded at any of the three subareas, but several state species of concern or fully protected species were recorded in low numbers including burrowing owl, long-eared owl ( _Asio otus_ ), loggerhead shrike ( _Lanius ludovicianus_ ), Vaux’s swift ( _Chaetura vauxi_ ), northern harrier ( _Circus cyaneus_ ), tricolored blackbird ( _Agelaius tricolor_ ), LeConte’s thrasher ( _Toxostoma lecontei_ ), and golden eagle. Two inactive raptor nests and a single active burrowing owl burrow were found during nest searches. Based on the results of sensitive wildlife surveys and nest searches, M.H. Wolf and Associates concluded that impacts to sensitive species and nesting raptors from the construction and operation of the proposed wind-energy facility would not be significant.

## _WEST – 2009_

WEST conducted additional baseline avian use surveys within the three subareas comprising the Project (Figure 1). The avian use surveys consisted of 30-min fixed-point surveys (variable circular plots) conducted using methods described by Reynolds et al. (1980), and are consistent with recommendations presented in the Guidelines (CEC and CDFG 2007). The objective of these avian use surveys is to estimate the seasonal, spatial, and temporal use of the study area by birds, particularly raptors, and to verify the results of the M.H. Wolfe and Associates analysis. Survey points were selected to achieve optimal coverage of the study area and habitats within the study area, and were established with an approximate density of 1.0 to 1.5 points per square mile (0.6 to 0.9 per square kilometer), as recommended in the Guidelines. Sampling intensity was designed to document bird use and behavior by habitat and season within the study area. Surveys began on February 2, 2009 and will continue on a weekly basis through June 30, 2009.

In May, WEST summarized the results of the fixed-point surveys for the first half of the study period, from February 2 to April 16, 2009. Based on data collected during the winter period (February 2 – March 15), raptor use (number of raptors divided by total number of surveys) was 0.33 birds/20-min survey in the CPC Proper and 0.09 in the CPC East; no raptors were observed in the Ward Subarea. During the spring period (March 16 – April 16) mean raptor use was 0.45 birds/20-min survey in the CPC Proper, 0.04 in the CPC East, and 0.20 in the Ward Subarea.

Based on the results from other wind-energy facilities across the US, WEST developed a ranking of seasonal and annual mean raptor use as: low (0 – 0.5 birds/survey); low to moderate (0.5 – 1.0); moderate (1.0 – 2.0); high (2.0 – 3.0); and very high (> 3.0). Raptor use in the Project during winter and spring of 2009 was low, relative to data collected at other existing and proposed wind-energy facilities (see Figure 2 for a comparison of annual and seasonal mean raptor use at US wind-energy facilities). These results are consistent with the low use figures reported by M.H. Wolfe and Associates.

## **Regional Avian Use and Mortality Studies**

## _Nexrad Radar Study for the PDV Wind Project_

The PDV Wind-Energy Project is located approximately eight miles (13 kilometers) to the southwest of the Project. An avian radar screening assessment was conducted by Detect, Inc. for the PDV project in 2006 (Detect 2006). The purpose of the assessment was to develop data on levels of nocturnal migratory bird activity in the project area and reference areas during the fall and spring migration periods. The assessment was based on archived remote sensing data from the National Weather Service (NWS) WSR 88-D Next Generation Radar (NEXRAD) from the Edwards Air Force Base, in California. The assessment compared metrics of bird migration intensity at the proposed site with ten reference areas that were located equidistance from the radar location (see Figure 2 of the PDV report for the approximate location of the evaluation areas). Site 1, which contains the PDV site, ranked 5[th ] lowest out of the 11 sites investigated during spring migration and 2[nd] lowest during fall migration. Of the 11 sites investigated, the proposed Project is nearest the PDV evaluation site (Site 1). The highest migration intensity was observed primarily at the sites to the south and east of the PDV project and the Project. Based on the literature review of studies focused on migrant flight altitude, the PDV report concluded that a wind-energy facility at the site is not likely to significantly impact nocturnal migrants. Additionally, mean migration flight altitudes at the sites ranged from 410 to 2,000 m (1,345 to 6,562 ft), well above the maximum turbine height of 122 m (400 ft). We believe the same conclusions would apply to the Alta-Oak Creek Mojave Project.

_Nocturnal Radar Studies for an Unpublished WEST Report_

A nocturnal radar study was conducted by WEST in 2006 at a site located directly to the northeast of the Project (WEST, unpublished data). The purpose of the nocturnal radar study was to characterize avian migration over the site and to compare the relative magnitude of nocturnal migration over the proposed development area with other sites. Radar surveys were designed to collect baseline information on passage rates and flight altitude of nocturnal migrants at a location representative of the proposed development area. A single mobile radar lab consisting of a Furuno FR 1510-MKIII marine radar mounted on a vehicle was used for a continuous 30–day period during the spring. The radar was an X-band, transmitting at 9,410 MHz with peak power output of 12 kW, similar to other radar labs used to study wind-energy development sites throughout the US (Cooper et al. 1991; Harmata et al. 1999; Roy and Pelletier 2005).

Data collected over 260 hours of data collection during the spring radar study showed that nocturnal migrant passage rates at the site are among the lowest of any wind resource area (WRA) studied. Similar spring radar data are available for eight WRAs in the eastern US and three in the western or Midwestern US. Horizontal passage rates in the eastern US ranged from 110–404 targets/km/hour and averaged 222 targets/km/hour, which is substantially higher than the 69 targets/km/hour observed at the study site. Of the three radar studies conducted in the Midwest or western US, two had higher passage rates (93–98 targets/km/hour) and only one project (Stateline on the Oregon/Washington border; 50 targets/km/hour) had lower passage rates than the study site.

## _Avian Use Surveys for an Unpublished WEST Report_

Avian use surveys were conducted by WEST in 2005-2006 at the site described above (WEST, unpublished data. Twenty-min fixed-point avian use surveys were conducted within 800-m (2,623 ft) radius plots surrounding eight observation points within the site. During spring and summer each point was surveyed four times per week (twice in the morning and twice in the afternoon), and during summer and winter all points were surveyed twice every two weeks (once in the morning and once in the afternoon). Over the course of the study, 91 species of birds were observed during 1,048 point count surveys conducted over 67 visits to the site. During the study, 13,254 individual birds within 8,263 groups were recorded.

Waterbirds and shorebirds had very low use during all seasons. Raptor/vulture use was generally higher during fall (0.64 birds/20-min survey), winter (0.60), and spring (0.58), and lower during summer (0.14). In fall and winter, buteos (hawks) made up the majority of the raptor/vulture use, while turkey vultures ( _Cathartes aura_ ) were the most abundant raptor/vulture species in spring. Upland gamebirds had the highest use in winter (1.70 birds/20-min survey) and fall (1.30), and lower in spring (0.49) and summer (0.33). Passerines had the highest use of any bird type in the fall (13.39 birds/20-min survey), winter (11.43), spring (9.76) and summer (5.88).

Mean annual raptor/vulture use at the study site was 0.49 birds/plot/20-min survey, with 23% of this value comprised of use by turkey vultures in spring and fall (no vultures were observed in summer or winter). Excluding use by vultures, mean annual raptor use at the study site was 0.38 birds/plot/20-min survey. Based on a comparison of the results from 36 other wind-energy facilities that implemented similar survey protocols a ranking of mean annual raptor use was developed as: low (0 – 0.5 raptors/plot/20-min survey); low to moderate (0.5 – 1.0); moderate (1.0 – 2.0); high (2.0 – 3.0); and very high (> 3.0). Under this ranking, annual use at the study site would be considered low, ranking 24[th] (see Figure 2e).

Based on data collected during the study, raptor use in the area is substantially lower than that observed at the Altamont Pass and Solano County wind-energy facilities in California, and is lower than most other facilities evaluated throughout the western and Midwestern US. This is to be expected given the limited habitat quality of creosote ( _Larrea tridentata_ ) scrub found on the Project relative to the high rodent densities found in the non-native grasslands of the Altamont WRA. Very few raptors nest in the region, relatively few raptors migrate through the area, and few raptors winter on the Project. It is expected that mean raptor use (number of raptors divided by the number of 800-m plots and the total number of surveys) at the Project will be similar to this study site, with some areas possibly having low to moderate avian use using the above ranking system. Based on fixed-point bird use surveys, use of the site by all bird species combined was also lower than many other wind-energy facilities evaluated throughout the US. Studies conducted by Anderson et al. (2004) in the Tehachapi Pass WRA (see discussion below) support the general conclusions that this region likely poses a low risk to birds compared to other wind-energy facilities in the US.

_Avian Use and Mortality Study in the Tehachapi Pass WRA--Anderson et al. 2004_

The primary objective of the study was to estimate and compare avian use, fatality rates and collision risk indices among factors such as bird taxonomic group), turbine type, and turbine location within the operating Tehachapi Pass WRA between October 1996 and May 1998

(Anderson et al. 2004). Anderson et al. (2004) divided the Tehachapi Pass WRA into three geographic locations, the West Ridge, the Middle Ridge and the East Slope (see Figure 1). At the time of the study, approximately 3,300 turbines were operating in the WRA. A total of 3,318 5- min bird utilization counts, including 1,404 at the West Ridge, 992 at the Middle Ridge, and 922 at the East Slope, as well as 829 carcass searches, were completed in the Tehachapi Pass WRA from October 2, 1996 to May 27, 1998.

## General Avian Use, Frequency Occurrence and Species Composition

Avian use (mean number of individuals per survey) across all three geographic locations was highest in the spring (1.61 birds/5-min survey), followed by fall (1.55), winter (1.20) and summer (0.93). The highest use occurred at the West Ridge in spring (2.36 birds/5-min survey) and the lowest use was recorded at the East Slope in summer (0.35). Raptor use was generally higher during the fall (0.04 birds/5-min survey) and winter (0.03) and slightly lower during the spring and summer (0.02). Raptor use was lowest in the summer and there were no raptors observed during winter at the East Slope.. Passerine abundance was highest during fall (1.14 birds/5-min survey) and lowest during summer (0.59) with similar values for spring (0.86) and winter (0.79). Passerines had the highest mean use at the East Slope during fall (1.65 birds/5-min survey).

Mean utilization rates by bird type were calculated for each geographic location within the study area. Similar patterns of use were observed at all locations, with some variations in the proportions of use by bird types in the different locations. The highest total bird use was observed at the West Ridge (1.64 birds/5-min survey), followed by East Slope (1.08), and Middle Ridge (0.95). Raptors showed similar use at both the West Ridge (0.04 birds/5-min survey) and Middle Ridge (0.04); however, this bird type had significantly (p < 0.10) lower use at the East Slope (0.01). The highest use by corvids was observed at the West Ridge (0.51). Significantly (p < 0.10) lower use by corvids was observed at the Middle Ridge (0.25) and significantly (p < 0.10) lower use was again observed at East Slope (0.11). Passerines showed no significant difference in use between the West Ridge (0.94 birds/5-min survey), the Middle Ridge (0.61), and the East Slope (0.92) (p > 0.10). There were no significant differences in use between the West Ridge (0.15 birds/5-min survey), Middle Ridge (0.05), and East Slope (0.04) for other birds (p > 0.10).

## Avian Fatality Counts and Composition

One hundred twenty-seven (127) avian fatalities representing 27 species were identified during carcass searches at the Tehachapi Pass WRA, with 75 of the 127 fatalities found within search plots. In addition, one long-eared bat ( _Plecotus auritus_ ) fatality with a fresh wound to the body was found three m (9.8 ft) from a turbine at West Ridge during a carcass search.

Forty-four of the 127 fatalities (34.6%) were raptors. Raptor species with the most fatalities were the red-tailed hawk ( _Buteo jamaicensis_ ; 14), great horned owl ( _Bubo virginianus_ ; 13), and American kestrel ( _Falco sparverius_ ; nine). Other raptor fatalities consisted of two barn owls ( _Tyto alba_ ) and single fatalities of ferruginous hawk ( _Buteo regalis_ ), prairie falcon ( _Falco mexicanus_ ), long-eared owl, flammulated owl ( _Otus flammeolus_ ), an unidentified buteo, and unidentified raptor. Only two corvid species were found as fatalities, common raven ( _Corvus corax_ ; eight) and scrub jay ( _Aphelocoma californica_ ; two), representing 7.9% of the total.

Twenty-seven of the fatalities (21.3%) were passerines. Passerine species with the most fatalities included western meadowlark ( _Sturnella neglecta_ ; six), horned lark ( _Eremophila alpestris_ ; three), European starling ( _Sturnus vulgaris_ ; three), white-crowned sparrow ( _Zonotrichia leucophrys_ ; two), and dark-eyed junco ( _Junco hyemalis_ ; two). Other passerine fatalities consisted of single fatalities of chipping sparrow ( _Spizella passerina_ ), Brewer’s blackbird ( _Euphagus cyanocephalus_ ), hermit thrush ( _Catharus guttatus_ ), rock wren ( _Salpinctes obsoletus_ ), yellowrumped warbler ( _Dendroica coronata_ ), loggerhead shrike and unidentified sparrow in addition to four unidentified passerine fatalities. Other birds comprised 46 (36.3%) of the fatalities. Other bird species with fatalities included the rock pigeon ( _Columba livia_ ; 11), mourning dove ( _Zenaida macroura_ ; six), northern flicker ( _Colaptes auratus_ ; three), greater roadrunner ( _Geococcyx californianus_ ; two), chukar ( _Alectoris chukar_ ; two), and California quail ( _Callipepla californica_ ; two). Twenty fatalities remained unidentified to taxonomic group and were grouped in the other bird category.

Most of the 127 avian fatalities occurred at West Ridge (91 fatalities; 71.7%), followed by the East Slope (19; 15.0%), and the Middle Ridge (16; 12.6%). One additional passerine fatality was located between the Middle Ridge and East Slope. Raptor fatalities were proportionately higher at the East Slope (9 of 19 fatalities; 47.4%) than at West Ridge (32 of 91; 35.2%) or the Middle Ridge (three of 16; 18.8%). Corvids were consistently the lowest fatality type overall and at each geographical location. Passerines were higher proportionately at Middle Ridge (seven of 16 fatalities; 43.8%) and East Slope (six of 19; 31.6%), compared to the West Ridge (13 of 91; 14.3%).

Overall, the West Ridge had the highest avian mortality (0.145 carcasses/survey), followed by the Middle Ridge (0.053) and the East Slope (0.041). Mortality at West Ridge was significantly (p < 0.10) higher than mortality at either the Middle Ridge or East Slope.

Patterns of mortality varied across geographic location with respect to taxonomic group. For the West Ridge, mortality was very similar for raptors (0.056 carcasses/survey) and other birds (0.057). Lower mortality was observed for passerines (0.025); however, this difference was not significant (p > 0.10). Corvid fatality (0.008 carcasses/survey) was significantly (p < 0.10) lower than either raptor or other bird fatality; however, corvid fatality was not significantly different from passerine fatality. For the Middle Ridge, fatality was highest for other birds (0.024 carcasses/survey), followed by corvids (0.014), passerines (0.009), and raptors (0.006). None of the observed fatality rates by taxonomic group were significantly different among groups. For the East Slope, similar mortality rates were observed for raptors (0.012 carcasses/survey), passerines (0.016), and other birds (0.012).

## Annual Fatality Estimates

The study by Anderson et al. (2004) was not specifically designed to provide standardized estimates of avian mortality and the wide interval between searches (90 days) lead to a high level of uncertainty in the fatality estimates. Additionally, the unknown impact scavenging had on the fatality estimates could greatly impact the fatality estimates. With these obvious caveats in mind, the unadjusted estimate of raptor fatalities for the Tehachapi Pass WRA, as reported by Anderson at al. (2004), was 0.047 raptors/turbine/year. The average nameplate output of the

turbines in the sample was 0.19 kW, yielding an estimate of 0.25 raptors/MW/year unadjusted for searcher efficiency bias, and 0.3 raptors/MW/year adjusted for searcher efficiency bias.

Raptor use is the clearest factor related to raptor fatality at the Tehachapi Pass WRA. The West Ridge had the highest raptor use and by far the highest fatality rates, while the Middle Ridge had moderate raptor use and moderate fatality rates, and the East Slope had very low raptor use and very low raptor fatality rates. At a macro scale, raptor use of a WRA still appears to be one of the most important factors that can be easily measured and is generally related to risk of collision. At the Tehachapi Pass WRA, there were differences in raptor use geographically that could be measured and were related to fatality rates. These results support the collection of baseline data within diverse and large wind-energy facilities for use in estimating locations of least impact.

The Project is in close proximity to the three regions of the Tehachapi Pass WRA studies by Anderson et al. (2004; Figure 1). It is expected that the CPC East Subarea would have use and fatality rates comparable to those observed at the East Slope of the Tehachpai Pass WRA, while the expected use and mortality at the western portions of the CPC Proper and Ward Subareas are expected to be somewhat higher and comparable to those observed at the Middle and West Ridge of the Tehachapi Pass WRA.

## _Fatality Monitoring at the Alite Wind-Energy Facility_

The Alite Wind-Energy Facility (Alite WEF) is located in the immediate vicinity of the Project, between the CPC East and CPC Proper Subareas. An avian and bat fatality monitoring study was initiated by Oak Creek Energy Systems at Alite in June of 2008. All eight turbines, two guyed meteorological (met) towers, and a power line were searched for avian and bat carcasses, or evidence of a fatality, approximately three times per week from June 9, 2008 through May 15, 2009. At turbines, searches were conducted along parallel transects situated at 30, 90, 150, and 210 ft (9, 27, 46, and 64 m) from the center-line of the turbine string. At the met towers, searches were conducted along three circular transects encompassing the tower at 30, 90, and 150 ft from the tower. At the power line, a single transect 30 ft from the center line was searched on each side of the power line.

Over the course of the study, a total of eight fatalities were found: four at the met tower, three at turbines, and one beneath the power line. Fatalities found at the met tower included two western meadowlarks found in July, a single lark sparrow ( _Chondestes grammacus_ ) found in September, and a single white-throated swift ( _Aeronautes saxatalis_ ) found in October. Fatalities found at turbines consisted of a California quail and an unidentified bird found at Turbine #3 in November, and an unidentified bird at Turbine #4 in January. The single fatality found at the power line was a common raven found in September.

Searcher efficiency trials were conducted on 18 separate dates throughout the year. Of the 230 carcasses placed within survey plots during trials, 193 were found by searchers, leading to a searcher detection rate of 83.9%. Scavenger removal trials were conducted during winter, spring, summer, and fall beginning April 2007 and ending January 2008 by M.H. Wolfe and Associates on the Oak Creek Energy site and the CPC East Subarea, which are adjacent to the Alite WindEnergy Facility. By the end of day six of the trials, 62.5% of the carcasses had been removed. No bat carcasses were used for searcher efficiency or scavenger removal trials and separate

estimates for large and small birds were not calculated. Additionally, scavenger removal trials were conducted outside of the study site in an area without turbines. With these caveats in mind, a very rough estimate of avian mortality at the Alite WEF, adjusted for searcher efficiency and scavenger removal is 1.06 birds per turbine, met tower, or power line per year. Given the 3.0 MW output of turbines at the Alite facility, this equates to 0.35 birds/MW/year, which is on the low end compared to other wind-energy facilities throughout the US (see Figure 3). In addition, no raptors were found during the study, so the raptor mortality estimate is 0.

Regardless of the uncertainty surrounding the estimate, the very low number of avian fatalities and absence of bat fatalities encountered during the carcass searches suggests relatively low levels of mortality at the Alite facility. To allow for more accurate estimates of seasonal and annual avian and bat mortality, a second year of fatality monitoring is warranted, and is consistent with recommendations in the Guidelines (CEC and CDFG 2007).

WEST will initiate a second year of monitoring at the Alite facility in the early summer of 2009. The study will consist of standardized carcass searches at all eight turbines and two met towers. Searches will be conducted on a twice monthly basis during summer (May 16 – July 31) and winter (November 1 – March 15), and on a weekly basis during the spring (March 16 – May 15) and fall (August 1 – October 31) migration seasons. Searches at each turbine will be conducted within a square 200 m (656 ft) by 200 m plot with the turbine at the center. Plots at each met tower will be 120 m (394 ft) by 120 m, centered on the tower. Plots will be searched along parallel transects spaced six-10 m (20-33 ft) apart (depending on detection ability), with the orientation of the transects based on the orientation of the topography surrounding the turbines. In addition to standardized carcass searches, searcher efficiency and scavenger removal trials will be conducted on multiple dates during each season to account for varying stages of vegetation, weather, climatic conditions, and scavenger densities.

## **CONCLUSION**

The results of site-specific and regional avian studies conducted to date support the general conclusion that this region likely poses a low risk to birds compared to other wind-energy facilities in the US. Avian use data collected by M.H. Wolf and associates (2009a, 2009b, 2009c) and avian use and fatality data collected by Anderson et al. (2004), while generally not directly comparable to those collected at the majority of modern wind-energy facilities in the US, suggest relatively low numbers of raptors and birds use the project subareas. The site specific avian use data collected at the subareas and data collected nearby (WEST unpublished data), which are more comparable to most other studies at wind-energy facilities, support the low raptor use and low overall bird use at this site.  In addition, the fatality data collected at the Alite facility has documented low overall bird mortality and no raptor or bat mortality over the one year of study to date.

The large amount of data collected at the site, including mortality information which is a more direct measure of impacts, and the nearby nocturnal migrant studies, all indicate that mortality levels (number/MW/yr) will be in the low range compared to other projects.  Post-construction studies will be conducted to estimate the level of mortality.
